strengths: Soundness: The paper presents a coherent data pipeline with concrete filtering rules, minimal unique Search/Replace construction, and round-trip application checks. Controlled results show substantial gains over Base+SFT and a token-matched StarCoder2-style baseline on SWE-bench Lite and Verified.

Evaluation: Useful ablations separately examine Search/Replace formatting, linked-issue context, error-driven augmentation, and Python-only versus multilingual mid-training. Intermediate localization, patch-validity, HumanEval, and LiveCodeBench results provide evidence beyond end-to-end SWE-bench Pass@1.

Significance: A corpus of roughly 2.0M PRs and 17.7B tokens across 12 languages would be a valuable resource. The finding that structured PR mid-training improves repository editing under a relatively simple inference pipeline is practically important.

Originality: The individual ingredients are familiar, but combining large-scale PR/issue linking, verified Search/Replace targets, repository-balanced sampling, and Agentless-aligned SFT constitutes a meaningful data-centric contribution.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. The appendix supplies prompts, training hyperparameters, language statistics, schemas, filtering heuristics, and a pipeline algorithm. It also candidly notes the single-model and non-agentic-evaluation limitations.
weaknesses: Soundness: The paper calls examples “verified,” but verification only establishes that Search/Replace blocks reproduce the observed PR diff; it does not verify that the change is semantically correct or resolves the linked issue. Merged/approved status is only a noisy proxy, and no manual quality audit quantifies incorrect issue links, bot-filter errors, or low-quality accepted PRs.

The evaluation-contamination analysis is incomplete. Repository and content decontamination are described for the PR mid-training corpus, but the SFT data are derived from SWE-Gym, SWE-rebench, and SWE-bench-Live, with no demonstrated instance-, patch-, issue-, or repository-level deduplication against SWE-bench Lite and Verified. Because SFT uses ground-truth repair trajectories, possible overlap is a material threat to the central results.

The causal analysis remains confounded. The StarCoder2-style baseline differs in formatting, filtering, issue context, and sampling. Table 8 isolates format and issue context within the Python Clean-PR subset, but there is no clean ablation of the filtering/verification pipeline or repository sampling. Thus the paper cannot firmly attribute the full improvement to the claimed corpus-quality mechanisms.

Evaluation breadth is limited to one model family and two overlapping, Python-only SWE-bench splits. There is no multilingual repository benchmark despite training on 12 languages, no evaluation with an agentic scaffold, and no independent training seeds or uncertainty estimates. Comparisons with external systems use copied results under differing models and frameworks, so claims of SOTA performance and reduced dependence on scaffolding are stronger than the evidence supports.

Several interpretations are overstated: the multilingual result also increases training tokens from 3.8B to 17.7B, so it does not establish cross-language transfer; improved patch validity may primarily reflect train/test output-format alignment; and Best-of-N is reported without a selection mechanism, so it is an oracle Pass@k result rather than a deployable improvement.

Reproducibility is only partial. The dataset and presumably artifacts are promised for future release, but no accessible code, data, checkpoints, crawl snapshot, or exact data split identifiers are provided. Reproducing the reported model also requires roughly 10.8 days on 32 H200 GPUs. Important implementation details such as loss masking and dataset mixing are unclear.

Ethics and data governance need substantially more treatment. The impact statement briefly mentions licensing and attribution, but permissive-license and opt-out filtering are specified only for the StarCoder2 baseline, not clearly for Clean-PR itself. The paper does not adequately address redistribution rights, preservation or anonymization of contributor comments and issue text, personal information, takedown procedures, or license propagation in the planned release.

There are minor consistency and writing issues, including the text reporting 10.3% for Base+SFT on Lite while Table 6 reports 11.3%, and awkward or contradictory phrasing about outperforming other systems “besides requiring heavy agent scaffolding.”

strengths: Soundness: The round-trip construction is a strong aspect of the work: Search/Replace blocks must be unique, non-overlapping, and reconstruct the target file bit-for-bit. The manuscript also describes repository-, file-, and n-gram-level decontamination for the mid-training corpus.

Evaluation: The compute-matched StarCoder2-style baseline (17.4B versus 17.7B tokens), Python-subset format/intent ablations, and error-augmentation ablation are useful controls. The reported gains are substantial, including 20.4% to 30.6% on SWE-bench Verified relative to the compute-matched baseline.

Significance and originality: Constructing approximately two million verified PR examples across 12 languages could be a valuable community contribution. Combining linked issue intent, pre-change code, and executable edits at this scale is more distinctive than merely collecting additional commits.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper is generally clear and includes corpus statistics, prompts, training hyperparameters, inference constraints, and a dataset schema. It also honestly acknowledges the single-model and non-agentic evaluation limitations. weaknesses: Soundness/claim alignment: Clean-PR training receives the files actually modified by each PR, restricts examples to at most five core files, and averages only 1.7 modified files. Repository-wide file localization is instead learned from benchmark-derived SFT trajectories. Consequently, the experiments support improved edit generation under selected context more directly than the central claim that PR mid-training internalizes repository-level navigation and editing capability.

Contamination risk: Decontamination is described for Clean-PR, but the 75,082-example SFT set is drawn from SWE-bench-Live, SWE-rebench, and SWE-Gym, and the paper does not explain how these trajectories were checked against SWE-bench Lite/Verified. It reports neither overlap-removal counts nor temporal cutoffs. Because these sources can involve closely related repositories and code histories, this omission materially weakens confidence in the headline results.

Attribution remains confounded: The StarCoder2-style control differs simultaneously in filtering, sampling, formatting, retained file types, and issue linkage. Table 8 separates format and issue linkage only on the Python subset and does not isolate verification or filtering. Likewise, the claimed benefit of multilingual training compares 17.7B tokens against 3.8B Python tokens, so language diversity is confounded with substantially more training data.

Evaluation is too narrow for the broad conclusions: Results come from one 32B architecture and two closely related, static Python benchmark variants. There are no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, statistical tests, detailed failure analysis, or evaluation on multilingual and temporally fresh repo-level tasks. Comparisons to external systems copy numbers obtained under different training and inference conditions.

Several interpretations are overstated or technically questionable. Unified diffs do not depend solely on exact line numbers—their context supports offset application—so the paper's characterization of them as intrinsically line-number-fragile is misleading. Higher oracle Pass@10 also does not by itself demonstrate intrinsic reasoning ability or an effective deployable reranking procedure. There is additionally a 10.3% versus 11.3% inconsistency for the Base+SFT Lite result.

Reproducibility is presently conditional: the dataset is only promised for future release, and no code, trained checkpoint, exact crawl snapshot, or executable processing pipeline is identified. Reproducing the main run also requires roughly 259 hours on 32 H200 GPUs, making the missing artifacts especially consequential.

Ethics and data governance are insufficiently resolved. The Clean-PR filtering specification does not exclude non-permissively licensed repositories or honor opt-outs, even though the StarCoder2 baseline explicitly does so. Public availability is not permission to redistribute code. PR descriptions and comments may also contain personal or sensitive information, but the paper specifies no privacy screening or anonymization for Clean-PR. The impact statement acknowledges licensing in general terms without providing a concrete release policy.

strengths: Soundness: The central result is supported by strong controlled comparisons. With the same Qwen2.5-Coder-32B base and downstream SFT, Clean-PR mid-training reaches 24.3%/30.6% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Lite/Verified, versus 15.7%/20.4% for the approximately token-matched StarCoder2-style corpus and 11.3%/17.6% without mid-training. Improvements in patch validity and localization provide useful supporting evidence beyond end-to-end scores.

Originality: Converting large-scale pull requests into minimal, uniquely anchored Search/Replace blocks with exact round-trip reconstruction is a valuable and reasonably novel data-engineering contribution. Coupling this with linked issue context makes the supervision better aligned with repository-level repair than ordinary commit or diff corpora.

Significance: A verified corpus of roughly 2.0M training PRs across 12 languages and 45,267 repositories would be a substantial community resource. The finding that data-centric mid-training can materially improve a relatively simple inference pipeline is important for separating model capability from agent-scaffold complexity.

The Python-subset ablations provide credible evidence for both linked issue context and Search/Replace formatting: removing either lowers Verified Pass@1 from 27.8% to 25.7% and 24.4%, respectively. Error-driven SFT augmentation also consistently improves both benchmarks and line localization.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear and well organized, with informative corpus statistics, concrete examples, exact inference prompts, training hyperparameters, and an explicit discussion of single-model and non-agentic-evaluation limitations.
The manuscript recognizes security, malicious-use, licensing, and attribution risks rather than concealing them; these concerns are appropriate and do not by themselves count against the work.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is presently incomplete. The manuscript says that the corpus “will” be released but provides no accessible artifact, code, dataset identifier, model checkpoint, or release license. Reproducing the reported model also requires about 259 hours on 32 H200 GPUs, making the promised data, preprocessing implementation, checkpoints, and evaluation outputs especially important.

The decontamination account does not clearly establish that the SFT sources—SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym, and, according to Table 5, SWE-bench-Live—are disjoint from Lite and Verified at the instance, repository, and temporal levels. Appendix A.6 appears focused on Clean-PR mid-training and reports neither removal counts nor audits. Because the external/SOTA comparison depends on absolute benchmark scores, this should be documented explicitly.

Generality is limited: all training experiments use one 32B model, and end-to-end evaluation is confined to the Python-only SWE-bench Lite and Verified sets despite the claimed 12-language benefit. The all-language versus Python comparison also changes training volume from 3.8B to 17.7B tokens, so it does not isolate multilingual transfer; the claim that diverse syntax improves abstract reasoning is therefore speculative.

No repeated runs, confidence intervals, or per-instance significance tests are reported. This is particularly relevant for the 300-example Lite set and for smaller ablation differences. The paper should also define file and line accuracy mathematically and explain aggregation when multiple files or locations are valid.

The external comparison in Table 7 is only contextual: systems differ in base models, training data, inference frameworks, and compute, while values are copied from prior papers. It does not substantiate strong statements that Clean-PR itself outperforms complex agentic approaches or “bridges the scaling gap” under controlled conditions.

The filtering rule accepts PRs that are “MERGED or APPROVED,” although approved-but-unmerged changes are not necessarily accepted or correct. Moreover, exact patch application proves formatting consistency, not semantic correctness. A manual quality audit or executable-test study is needed to support the repeated characterization of the corpus as high-quality supervision.

Ethical/data-governance treatment is too brief for an intended large-scale public release. The main Clean-PR pipeline does not specify license filtering, author opt-outs, handling of personal information in descriptions/comments, or takedown procedures; notably, permissive-license and opt-out filtering is described for the StarCoder2 baseline but not clearly for Clean-PR.

There are minor consistency and writing problems: Table 6 reports 11.3% Lite for Base+SFT while the text states 10.3%, and several conclusion sentences are grammatically inverted or overstate causality. These do not undermine the core result but should be corrected.

strengths: Soundness: The data-construction pipeline is technically thoughtful. Reconstructing post-PR states, deriving minimal unique Search/Replace blocks, and requiring exact round-trip reconstruction provide a substantially stronger correctness check than merely collecting raw diffs.

Significance and originality: Using linked issues and accepted pull requests as large-scale supervision for intent-conditioned, multi-file editing is useful and timely. The reported corpus scale—2.0M training instances, 45,267 repositories, 12 languages, and 17.7B tokens—would make the dataset a valuable resource if released as described.

Evaluation: The main same-base-model comparisons show sizable improvements over SFT-only and token-matched StarCoder2-style mid-training: 30.6% versus 17.6% and 20.4% on SWE-bench Verified. The paper also evaluates 7B and 32B models, multilingual repair, an OpenHands agent, localization, patch validity, and general code benchmarks.

Ablations provide useful evidence: On the Python subset, linked issues and Search/Replace formatting each improve Verified performance, while error-driven augmentation improves both localization and end-to-end resolution across Python-only and multilingual training.

Presentation and partial reproducibility: The manuscript is generally clear and supplies dataset statistics, filtering rules, prompts, training hyperparameters, inference constraints, and an unusually substantive decontamination analysis, including repository exclusion, content matching, nearest-neighbor analysis, and manual inspection.
The impact statement recognizes security, licensing, and attribution risks, and the limitations section honestly identifies the under-representation of broad cross-cutting changes.
weaknesses: Soundness: Decontamination is documented only for Clean-PR, not for the 75,082-example SFT corpus derived from SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym, and SWE-bench-Live. The paper does not provide task- or repository-level overlap checks between these SFT sources and SWE-bench Lite/Verified. Because the final models are explicitly trained on ground-truth repairs from closely related SWE datasets, this is a material unresolved leakage risk for the headline benchmark scores and external comparisons.

The causal comparison is incompletely controlled. The StarCoder2-style baseline differs simultaneously in filtering, sampling, formatting, inclusion of non-code artifacts, and issue integration. Table 8 partially separates edit format and linked-issue context on Python, but omits the full factorial comparison under a common retained-example set and does not isolate the effects of verification and filtering. Thus, the paper supports the overall recipe better than its component-level explanations.

The claim that unified diffs become invalid when code shifts by one line is technically misleading: standard patch application uses context and commonly tolerates offsets or fuzz. The empirical format ablation is still useful, but the proposed explanation for the difference is overstated.

The mid-training corpus is only weakly repository-level: it retains the modified core files, caps examples at five such files, and supplies the target-file code rather than the broader repository or unmodified dependency context. Repository-wide localization is learned separately from benchmark-derived SFT. Claims that PR mid-training itself internalizes repository navigation should therefore be narrowed.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate for the main contribution. The paper says the dataset “will” or is “planned to” be released, but provides no accessible data, construction code, model checkpoints, exact crawl snapshot, instance identifiers, random seeds, or optimizer details such as weight decay and betas. The reported training requires roughly 9,500 H200 GPU-hours for the 32B stages, making released artifacts especially important.

No training-seed replication, confidence intervals, or paired significance tests are reported. Several ablation differences are only 2–4 percentage points on 300 or 500 instances, so their robustness to training and decoding variance remains uncertain.

The external comparisons in Table 7 combine different model sizes, training data, and inference frameworks using copied results. They contextualize performance but do not justify strong claims that Clean-PR itself surpasses competing methods or “bridges the scaling gap.”

Research ethics and data governance are insufficiently resolved. The proposed release contains repository identifiers, raw source files, PR descriptions, and reviewer comments. Unlike the StarCoder2-style baseline, the Clean-PR filtering description does not exclude non-permissive licenses or honor user opt-outs, nor does it specify PII removal, license preservation, takedown procedures, or consent safeguards. The impact statement notes licensing in general but does not mitigate these concrete release risks.

The limitations discussion is too narrow: it omits the possible SFT leakage, benchmark specialization, selection bias from merged/approved PRs, incomplete causal isolation, extreme compute cost, and the licensing/privacy concerns above. These issues prevent a weak-accept recommendation despite the paper’s strong empirical promise.

strengths: Significance: The work targets an important bottleneck in repository-level code editing and constructs a very large corpus: 3.05M validated PRs overall and a 2.02M-example, 17.7B-token training subset spanning 12 languages.

Soundness: Round-trip application, uniqueness checking, repository balancing, benchmark-repository exclusion, lexical decontamination, and the reported semantic-similarity analysis are valuable safeguards. The 32B results show large gains over the SFT-only and token-matched StarCoder2-style baselines on both SWE-bench Lite and Verified.

Evaluation breadth is strong: the manuscript includes 7B scaling, multilingual repair, OpenHands transfer, general-code benchmarks, edit-format and linked-issue ablations, error-augmentation ablations, and intermediate localization metrics.

Originality: Using linked PR/issue context as large-scale mid-training supervision is a useful synthesis. Search/Replace conversion itself is established, but applying verified reconstruction at this scale and combining it with error-driven Agentless-aligned SFT is meaningfully novel.

Presentation: The paper is generally well organized, visually polished, and unusually detailed about filtering rules, data schemas, prompts, training hardware, and high-level hyperparameters. The discussion honestly notes limited coverage of broad cross-cutting changes; that disclosure should not be penalized. weaknesses: Soundness: The central causal attribution remains under-controlled. The main Clean-PR versus StarCoder2-style comparison simultaneously changes filtering, repository sampling, edit representation, issue linking, and serialization. Table 8 partially separates representation and issue context on the Python subset, but lacks a fully crossed, token-matched ablation—particularly a Clean-PR-filtered Diff/PR-description condition—and never isolates the filtering and verification contribution.

Potential evaluation leakage is not resolved. Appendix A.6 describes decontamination of the Clean-PR corpus, but the final SFT data are drawn from SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym, and SWE-bench-Live, and the paper does not report task hashes, issue-date cutoffs, or explicit overlap checks between those SFT examples and Lite/Verified. Because this SFT directly teaches issue-resolution trajectories, its independence from the test sets is essential.

The semantic-leakage analysis is not strong evidence against contamination. A nonsignificant marginal correlation between nearest-neighbor similarity and success can be masked by task difficulty and does not establish the absence of leaked examples; only ten nearest pairs are manually examined. The collection cutoff is also unspecified.

Reported improvements have no uncertainty estimates, repeated training runs, or significance tests. Several ablation differences are only roughly 2–3 percentage points on 300 or 500 instances and may not be robust. The Pass@k experiment also omits sufficient sampling and estimator details.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate for the headline result. The dataset is only promised for future release, no code or checkpoint availability is stated, and important details are missing: the causal-loss masking/objective, optimizer parameters beyond peak learning rate, data order and seeds, SFT mixture/sampling weights, construction of positive trajectories and hard negatives, benchmark harness versions, and complete decoding settings. Reproducing the run additionally requires about 9,500 H200 GPU-hours for the reported 32B stages.

The paper overstates what validation establishes. Round-trip Search/Replace checking proves that a recorded change applies exactly; it does not establish that the PR is semantically correct, high quality, or that its tests pass. Likewise, unified diffs are described as inherently dependent on precise line-number prediction, although patch application also uses textual context and fuzzy matching. These claims should be narrowed.

The at-most-five-core-files rule, exclusion of added/deleted or mismatched files, top-three-file inference restriction, and aggressive extension filtering substantially narrow the meaning of “repository-level editing.” The evaluation does not stratify performance by edit size, number of files, new-file creation, or long-context demand, so the stated reduction in reliance on inference scaffolding has limited demonstrated scope.

Ethics and data governance are materially underdeveloped for an 8.6-TB GitHub crawl. Unlike the baseline appendix, the Clean-PR pipeline does not clearly specify license filtering, opt-out handling, personal-data removal, author/comment anonymization, retention policy, or how attribution and license obligations will be preserved in release. The brief impact statement acknowledges licensing but supplies no concrete mitigation.

Presentation has some consequential inconsistencies: the paper alternates among “largest publicly available,” “publicly released,” and “we plan to release”; it describes accepted changes while allowing MERGED or APPROVED status; and “3M,” “2M,” full-corpus, and training-corpus claims are sometimes blurred. These should be corrected before readers can assess the dataset contribution precisely.

strengths: Soundness: The paper presents strong evidence that PR-based mid-training is useful. On Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, Clean-PR improves Pass@1 over SFT-only from 11.3% to 24.3% on SWE-bench Lite and from 17.6% to 30.6% on Verified, while outperforming a token-matched 17.4B-token StarCoder2-style baseline.

The evaluation is unusually broad: it includes 32B and 7B models, Lite and Verified splits, Multi-SWE-bench Flash, an OpenHands transfer experiment, intermediate localization metrics, error-augmentation ablations, and HumanEval/LiveCodeBench checks for catastrophic forgetting.

The data pipeline is practically valuable and reasonably original in its combination of PR filtering, linked-issue augmentation, minimal unique Search/Replace construction, and round-trip reconstruction. The resulting 2.0M-example, 17.7B-token corpus would be a significant community resource if released as described.

The contamination analysis is substantially stronger than is typical: evaluation repositories are excluded, exact-file and patch/issue overlap filters are applied, and the appendix reports nearest-neighbor similarity analysis over all 500 Verified instances.

Presentation is clear and well organized. The main pipeline, dataset stages, prompts, training configuration, data schema, and high-level conversion algorithm are documented, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges that the five-file restriction under-represents broad cross-cutting changes.
The impact statement recognizes security, reliability, licensing, and attribution concerns rather than ignoring risks associated with automated repository modification.
weaknesses: The central causal attribution is not fully isolated. The primary StarCoder2-style comparison simultaneously changes edit format, filtering, issue context, and repository sampling. Table 8 separately studies format and issue context on the Python subset, but does not ablate the proposed filtering/verification decisions or provide a complete controlled factorial comparison.

Potential leakage through the Agentless-aligned SFT data is insufficiently documented. The main SFT corpus is derived from SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym, and SWE-bench-Live, but the explicit repository-, task-, and temporal-overlap guarantees are stated for Clean-PR and the multilingual SFT corpus, not clearly for this main SFT corpus. Because evaluation uses SWE-bench Lite and Verified, this should be audited and reported explicitly.

Statistical evidence is limited to single reported runs: there are no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the benchmark comparisons. The headline 8–10 point advantage over the token-matched baseline is persuasive, but several 2–3 point ablation and multilingual gains may be sensitive to evaluation or training variance.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The manuscript promises a future dataset release but does not commit clearly to releasing code, trained checkpoints, exact crawl snapshot/date, split manifests, and decontamination lists. It also omits details such as random seeds, optimizer betas/weight decay, sequence packing and loss masking, decoding limits, and precise definitions of file and line accuracy. Reproducing the main run additionally requires roughly 259 hours on 32 H200 GPUs.

The claim that repo-level capability is internalized into model weights is somewhat overstated. Clean-PR retains only changed core files, limits examples to at most five such files, and averages 1.7 modified files; downstream repository localization is learned through a separate benchmark-derived SFT stage and still uses an Agentless retrieval scaffold. The evidence supports improved repository editing priors more directly than broad repository understanding.

The paper occasionally overstates comparisons: external results are copied from papers using different scaffolds and training resources, so they do not establish a controlled state-of-the-art result. Likewise, calling the corpus already 'publicly available' conflicts with the statement that it 'will' be released.

The ethics discussion does not specify an actionable licensing and opt-out policy for Clean-PR. This is material because the proposed release includes repository identifiers, URLs, base code, PR text, comments, and edits. The StarCoder2 baseline explicitly filters non-permissive licenses and user opt-outs, whereas the Clean-PR pipeline does not state equivalent safeguards.
